title: "To be" and "to have" in the past
why: The verb "to be," missing in the present, really does exist in the past: הָיִיתִי, הָיָה, הָיְתָה… With it, you can say where you were, what it was like, and what you had (הָיָה לִי), making it agree with the thing you had.

{"lessons": ["

\"To be\" in the past: הָיָה

In the present, there's no verb \"to be\": אֲנִי בַּבַּיִת. In the past, it shows up: הָיִיתִי בַּבַּיִת (I was at home). It takes the endings you know, with an i before the ending. The verb עָשָׂה (to do, to make) follows exactly the same pattern.

Pronounto beto do
אֲנִיהָיִיתִי hayitiעָשִׂיתִי asiti
אַתָּההָיִיתָ hayitaעָשִׂיתָ asita
אַתְּהָיִית hayitעָשִׂית asit
הוּאהָיָה hayaעָשָׂה asa
הִיאהָיְתָה haytaעָשְׂתָה asta
אֲנַחְנוּהָיִינוּ hayinuעָשִׂינוּ asinu
אַתֶּםהֱיִיתֶם heyitemעֲשִׂיתֶם asitem
אַתֶּןהֱיִיתֶן heyitenעֲשִׂיתֶן asiten
הֵם / הֵןהָיוּ hayuעָשׂוּ asu

As always in the past, I doesn't change for gender: a man and a woman both say הָיִיתִי. Never say אֲנִי הָיָה or אֲנִי הָיְתָה! The question you'll hear everywhere: מָה עָשִׂיתָ? (to a man), מָה עָשִׂית? (to a woman), what did you do?

For \"you\" (plural), you'll often hear [hayitem] in conversation; [heyitem] is the careful form. And שָׁתִיתִי קָפֶה (I drank a coffee) [shatiti kafe] also follows the pattern of הָיִיתִי.

", "

What was it like?

To describe something, הָיָה agrees with the subject, like an adjective:

הַטִּיּוּל הָיָה מְעֻלֶּה.The trip was excellent. [ha-tiyul haya me'ule]
הַדִּירָה הָיְתָה קְטַנָּה.The apartment was small. [ha-dira hayta ktana]
הַחֲבֵרִים הָיוּ נֶחְמָדִים.The friends were nice. [ha-khaverim hayu nekhmadim]

With no subject, for \"it was,\" you use הָיָה (masculine singular). Where English says \"it was hot,\" Hebrew simply says \"was hot,\" with no \"it.\"

אֵיךְ הָיָה? — הָיָה כֵּיף, אֲבָל הָיָה חַם!How was it? — It was great, but it was hot! [eikh haya? — haya kef, aval haya kham!]

And the past of יֵשׁ / אֵין? הָיָה again, agreeing with whatever existed: הָיוּ שָׁם הַרְבֵּה אֲנָשִׁים (there were a lot of people), לֹא הָיָה מָקוֹם (there was no room).

", "

\"To have\" in the past: הָיָה לִי

You know that \"to have\" is יֵשׁ לִי, literally \"there is to me.\" In the past, יֵשׁ becomes הָיָה… and it agrees with the thing you have, not with the owner. English has nothing like this, so watch out!

The thing ownedHebrewPronunciationMeaning
masculineהָיָה לִי כֶּלֶבhaya li kelevI had a dog
feminineהָיְתָה לִי מְכוֹנִיתhayta li mekhonitI had a car
pluralהָיוּ לִי חֲבֵרִיםhayu li khaverimI had friends

The owner changes with לְ + suffix, as in the present: הָיָה לָנוּ, הָיְתָה לָהּ, הָיוּ לָהֶם… Negation: לֹא הָיָה לִי זְמַן (I didn't have time).

הָיְתָה לָנוּ חֻפְשָׁה מְעֻלָּה.We had an excellent vacation. [hayta lanu khufsha me'ula]

In conversation, you'll sometimes hear הָיָה לִי even before a feminine noun. Still, learn the agreement: it's the correct form, the one expected in writing.
